newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil state sees 1997/98 coffee crop down 40 pct.
newsitem.headline: Brazil state sees 1997/98 coffee crop down 40 pct.

text.p: The coffee harvest in Brazil's Minas Gerais state is set to fall to 8.3 million 60-kg bags in 1997/98 from a revised 13.8 million bags in 1996/97, the Agricultural Federation of Minas Gerais State (FAEMG) said.
"For 1997, the forecast in the state is for 8.3 million bags, with an average reduction of 40 percent," the FAEMG said in a statement.
Minas Gerais accounts for around half the total Brazilian coffee crop.

The expected drop was due to a bi-annual cycle which meant high crops were followed by lower ones, as well as high production costs, low productivity in some areas and financing problems, FAEMG president Rui Queiroz told reporters.
Queiroz said 700 million of the total 1.7 billion trees in the state were older than 15 years and produced fewer than 10 bags per hectare.
High production costs meant farmers were spending less on fertilizers and crop treatments, he added.
But FAEMG cautioned its forecast was preliminary and a new estimate would be issued in July or August 1997.
"(Caution) is recommended especially this year, as flowerings are very irregular. The margin of error of this forecast is between five and 10 percent," it said.
Plantings were expected to total 45,000 hectares in 1997, raising the total coffee area 5.5 percent from 1996. Planted area grew 9.8 percent during 1996.
FAEMG said it had revised upwards its estimate of the 1996/97 harvest to 13.8 million bags from 12.4 million after surveying 1,210 properties in Minas Gerais during December.
The south and west of the state accounted for most of the rise, it said.
